1:
The morning after Haman hangs opens on a double reversal, and the witnesses divide their attention between the estate that changes hands and the kinsman who at last steps into the light. The reformed John Gill notes that the house of Haman, with all the goods and estate belonging to it, was confiscated to the crown and given by the king to Esther — she who would have been the chief sufferer had his scheme prevailed; the Targum, Gill adds, swells the gift to take in the men of his house, all his treasures, and all his riches. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the house of Haman as the house with all that pertained to it, the property forfeited by his execution; and they mark the second movement of the verse, that Mordecai now came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her — her kinsman and foster-father, as Esther 2:7 had recorded.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the justice of the double grant. Adam Clarke observes that Haman, found guilty of treasonable practices, forfeited both life and goods, so that it was but just to confer his property, dignity, and office upon Mordecai, who had preserved the king's life and been the very object of Haman's malice. John Wesley reads the estate as justly forfeited to the king and no less justly bestowed on the queen, to compensate the danger to which Haman had exposed her; and he takes Mordecai's coming before the king to mean that he was admitted into the royal presence and family, made, as it seems, one of the seven princes. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott supplies the legal background: confiscation of goods necessarily followed a sentence of death in the East, as with us a convicted felon's property is forfeited to the Crown.

But it is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who draws the scene into its lessons. Here is Esther enriched: the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just, and what Haman would have done mischief with, Esther will do good with, for estates are to be valued as they are used — the word of Prov. 13:22 and Job 27:17. And here is Mordecai advanced, at last owned as the queen's cousin, though so humble and modest a man that he had concealed the relation and never used her interest for his own advantage. Who but Mordecai, Henry marvels, could have taken so little notice of so great an honour? See the vanity of laying up treasure upon earth, he adds from Ps. 39:6: he that heapeth up riches knoweth not who shall gather them — whether a friend, or, as here, the very enemy he hated above all men in the world.
2:
The ring passes from a dead traitor's hand to a faithful one, and the witnesses read in that small band of gold the transfer of the whole power of the empire. The reformed John Gill explains that the ring the king took from Haman and gave to Mordecai was, among the Persians, a token of the strongest affection and the strictest friendship; the Targum calls it his signet, the very seal with which laws, edicts, letters, and patents were signed, so that Mordecai was hereby made keeper of the seals. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the king took off the seal-ring he had taken from Haman — the same ring of Esther 3:10 — and by this act advanced Mordecai to the post of first minister, as Pharaoh had once advanced Joseph in Gen. 41:42; for the king's seal gave the force of law to an edict, taking the place of a signature.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the same point in plainer terms. Adam Clarke says that giving the ring, in which the royal seal was set, was tantamount to giving Mordecai the seal of the kingdom, and constituting him what a lord chancellor is among us. John Wesley reads it likewise: that ring which the king had formerly given to Haman he now gives to Mordecai, and with it the power whereof the ring was a sign, making him keeper of the signet. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enlarges the office: the ring constituted Mordecai the king's vizier, who would authenticate a royal decree and, having as it were carte blanche for the time, save his master all further trouble — a position, Ellicott observes, now become what Daniel's had been to Darius, that nobler servant to a worthier lord.

The second half of the verse turns from king to queen, and here the witnesses gather the estate and its steward into one providence. Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman — that is, Wesley explains, as her steward, to manage that great estate for her as he thought fittest; and so, Gill and Keil agree, the confiscated fortune and the confiscated office alike come to rest in the hands of the man Haman had built his gallows to destroy. What the enemy had heaped up in pride is handed, entire, to his intended victim: the treasures, the seal, the second place in the realm. The reader is meant to feel the completeness of the overturning — that in a single day the whole apparatus of Haman's greatness, the ring that had sealed the decree against the Jews included, is transferred to a Jew, and the very instrument of the death-warrant is now in the hand that will write the Jews' reprieve.
3:
With her enemy dead and her kinsman honoured, Esther finds her work only half done, and the witnesses gather around the tears with which she reopens it. The reformed John Gill notes that she went into the king's presence a second time without being called, as before, now with a new petition. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out what still stood against her people: the chief enemy was destroyed, but the edict written in the king's name, sealed with the royal seal, and published through all the provinces for the destruction of the Jews was still in force, and, having been issued in due legal form, could not by the laws of the Persians and Medes be revoked. So Esther fell down at his feet and besought him with weeping to do away with the mischief of Haman the Agagite and his device against the Jews; and the king held out to her the golden sceptre.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks how much more this cost her than the first approach. Her work was as yet only half done: she had seen the condemnation of her people's foe and the exaltation of her kinsman, but the royal edict still remained valid, a written decree sealed with the king's seal and supposed beyond the possibility of alteration. This was not a case in which Mordecai's newly-acquired dignity could authorise him to interfere; and so Esther, grown more courageous now that the ice was broken, makes a fresh appeal to the king to do the very thing that theoretically lay beyond the king's own power.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers over the affection and the theology of her intercession. Many a man's mischief survives him, he observes, and the wickedness he has devised goes on working when he is gone; it was not enough that Haman was hanged unless the mischief of Haman were put away too. She fell at the king's feet and begged with tears, every tear as precious as any of the pearls with which she was adorned; it was time to be earnest when the church of God lay at stake. Let none be so great as to be unwilling to stoop, Henry urges, nor so merry as to be unwilling to weep, when by it they may do any service to God's people. We read of no tears when Esther begged for her own life; but now, sure of that, she wept for her people, and tears of pity and tenderness are the most Christ-like of all. Those truly concerned for the public, he adds, would rather die in the last ditch than live to see the desolation of the church of God.
4:
For the second time the golden sceptre is stretched toward the kneeling queen, and the witnesses pause on that gesture of pardon before her petition is heard. The reformed John Gill reads the sceptre held out as a token that she had not incurred the king's displeasure by coming into his presence unsummoned, and that she was now admitted both to speak and to make her request. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the movement plainly: the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther, and Esther, so assured, arose from the feet where she had fallen and stood before the king — lifted from a mourner's posture to a petitioner's. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refers the reader back to the law that made the gesture necessary, the statute of Esther 4:11, by which any who came uncalled into the inner court went in peril of death unless the king extended the sceptre toward them.

That earlier law gives the verse its weight, for the witnesses have already felt how much hangs on the king's whim. Once already Esther had ventured her life on this same slender mercy and seen the sceptre held out to her in Esther 5:2; now, her own safety long secured and her enemy destroyed, she stakes herself upon the raised sceptre a second time, and not for herself but for her people. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, following her through the whole intercession, marks that she was encouraged to present her petition by the king's holding out the golden sceptre — the same encouragement, offered twice over, that emboldens a trembling suppliant to say at last what she has come to say.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very repetition is instructive. The sceptre extended a first time had saved her life; extended again, it invites her plea. Esther does not presume upon the favour she has already found; she comes as one still uncertain of her welcome, falls at the royal feet, and waits for the sign before she rises. And the sign is given: the despot whose unbending law could have cut her down instead reaches out the emblem of his clemency, and the queen stands. The reader who remembers whose hand it is that turns the hearts of kings will see in the lifted sceptre not merely a courtier's reprieve but the quiet working of a providence that has bent this arbitrary throne, twice over, toward the rescue of a doomed people. She rose, the witnesses note, not in the security of a favourite but in the boldness of one who has found grace, and stood before the king to plead a cause larger than her own life.
5:
Now the queen frames her actual request, and the witnesses attend to the careful wording with which she wraps it. The reformed John Gill notes the heap of phrases — if it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing seem right before the king, and I be pleasing in his eyes — all signifying much the same thing, piled up to work upon the king's affections and to show how submissive she was to his will. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that the introductory formulas, though like those she has used before, are here strengthened by two new phrases suited to so great and weighty a matter, so that she asks not merely that it please the king but that the thing itself be advisable and proper before him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott admires the skill of her petition. To reverse, he says, is rather to bring back, to recall; and Esther shows considerable art in her wording, for she avoids all mention of the king's own letters and speaks only of the letters, the device of Haman the Agagite, which he wrote. Yet it is to the king that the real injury is done, and she names it so — the device written to destroy the Jews which are in all the king's provinces. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same tact as a deliberate mercy toward the king's pride: she uses her various expressions to confirm his favour by a full submission to his pleasure, and she prudently takes the hatefulness of the whole action off the king and lays it upon Haman, who for his own ends had contrived the business and circumvented his master in it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson of her manner. Even when we have the utmost reason and justice on our side, and the clearest cause to plead, it becomes us to speak to our superiors with humility and modesty and all possible expressions of respect, and not to talk like those who demand when we are but suppliants. As soft answers turn away wrath, Henry says, so soft askings obtain favour; there is nothing lost by decency and good breeding. The witnesses converge on a single portrait of holy prudence: a queen with every right to be heard, choosing nonetheless to approach a proud and arbitrary man on her knees and in the gentlest terms, laying the guilt where it belonged and leaving the king an honourable path to undo what his own seal had sealed — wisdom, as Henry elsewhere says, taking a hard man by the right handle.
6:
Esther's plea rises now into open passion, and the witnesses hear in her double question the cry of a woman pleading for her own blood. The reformed John Gill paraphrases the anguish: I cannot bear it, it will break my heart; I shall die to see all my people massacred throughout the realm. He marks how she names the coming ruin — not a mere oppression but an utter destruction, an extermination — and how she calls them her kindred, a word of endearment, as being of the same family with her, so that she could not but sympathise in their distress. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the plea against what she has just confessed: she had now informed the king that she was cousin to Mordecai and therefore herself a Jewess, so that, though her own life and Mordecai's were no longer in danger with Haman dead, the decree still stood in full force against her people, and without repeal their destruction was inevitable.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the hinge on which the king's whole answer turns. He could not simply revoke the edict Haman had issued in due legal form; but, ready to perform the request of the queen, he first assures her of his good intentions before granting the remedy. Her question — how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people? — is the pressure that moves him, the queen refusing to divide her own safety from theirs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the tenderness of that refusal. Esther, a queen, owns her poor kindred, and speaks of them with a very tender concern; now it was that she mingled her tears with her words, wept, and made supplication. We read of no tears when she begged for her own life, but now that she was sure of that, she wept for her people. Tears of pity and tenderness, Henry says again, are the most Christ-like; those that are truly concerned for the public cannot bear to think of the destruction of their people and kindred, and therefore dare not omit any opportunity of giving them relief. The witnesses do not divide. They set before us a deliverer who will not be delivered alone — safe herself, adorned and enthroned, yet counting her own life little comfort if she cannot prevail for the lives of her kindred, and staking the favour she has won upon their reprieve.
7:
The king answers, and for the first time in the book he speaks to Esther and Mordecai together, the two whose lives Haman had sought now standing side by side before the throne. The reformed John Gill marks Mordecai's very presence in that audience, whether admitted at Esther's desire or by virtue of his new office, for he was now one of those that saw the king's face — a privileged place in the Persian court, from which Haman's fall had lately cleared the way. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the king's words as the preface to the permission he is about to grant: he could not himself revoke Haman's edict, but, ready to meet the queen's request, he first reminds them of what he has already done — given the house of Haman to Esther, and hanged Haman himself, because he laid his hand upon the Jews. Him they have hanged, the king says of his fallen favourite, as of a sentence already executed and just.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the speech the king pointing to the proofs of his own goodwill. Having shown his mind by hanging Haman for his scheme against the Jews and giving his property to Esther, the king now, though he shrinks from the outright reversal of a sealed decree, prepares to do what he can; his recital of past favours is the ground on which the new grant will stand. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same sense: the king had done enough already to convince them that he had a real concern for the Jewish nation, for he had ordered his own favourite to be hanged for laying his hand upon the Jews; and he therefore leaves it as fully with Esther and Mordecai to use his name and power for the Jews' deliverance as before he had left it with Haman to use that name and power for their destruction.

The witnesses do not divide, and the reversal they trace is exact. The very throne that had signed the death of a people now recites, as its own credentials, the death of the man who devised it. What Haman had, Mordecai now holds; what Haman did, the king now disowns; and the two intended victims are invited to take up the identical instruments — the royal name, the royal seal — that had lately been turned against them. The king's word is at once a confession and a commission: a confession that the enemy was justly destroyed for touching the Jews, and a commission to the Jews' own friends to write, in his name, whatever might now save them.
8:
Here the king lays bare the great constitutional knot of the book and, in the same breath, the way around it. The reformed John Gill takes the leave he gives simply: write ye also for the Jews as it liketh you — whatever may be thought fit and proper for their safety and security. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the principle the king cannot break: whatever had passed the royal signet could never be revoked, and no succeeding edict could repeal a preceding one; but an edict of similar force might be enacted for the Jews against their enemies, as the first had been against them, and thus the Jews be enabled to defend themselves and placed on an equal footing with their assailants. John Wesley, his fellow wesleyan-arminian, marvels at the folly of so rigid a law — the king could not recall the former letters because they were irrevocable by the law of the Medes and Persians — and observes how much more prudent is a constitution under which no law is made unrepealable; for it is God's prerogative, not a king's, not to repent, and to say what can never be altered or unsaid.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the mechanics of the workaround. Keil and Delitzsch note that the king grants Esther and Mordecai leave, as he had once granted Haman, to write in the king's name and seal with the king's ring as seems good to you — to put in writing whatever might, in their judgment, render Haman's edict harmless. Charles Ellicott sees Esther's first device, outright repeal, seen through and declined: such a writing may no man reverse, yet the king will do what he can, meeting the difficulty and saving the Jews without any formal reversal of the decree; and the upshot of the permission, whether the idea was the king's or Esther's or Mordecai's, was that the Jews were authorised to defend themselves.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the whole absurdity with a moralist's eye. That no decree once sealed could be repealed was reckoned a fundamental article of the realm's charter, echoed in the lions'-den law of Dan. 6:15; but it is ridiculous, Henry says, for any man or company of men to pretend to such infallibility of wisdom as to foresee all the consequences of what they decree, and it savours of that old presumption which ruined us all, We will be as gods. Yet the king found an expedient, signing a second decree to authorise the Jews to oppose force with force; and Henry notes the strange result — that the crown was driven to enact a civil war within its own borders, both sides taking up arms by the king's authority and yet against it. No better, he concludes, could come of men pretending to be wise above what is given them.
9:
The machinery of the counter-decree now grinds into motion, and the witnesses attend to its date, its reach, and the strange delay that had gone before. The reformed John Gill notes only that the king's scribes were called, as they had been called to write the former letter. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the fuller reckoning: the letters were prepared, just as Haman's had been, on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month Sivan, and written according to all that Mordecai commanded — sent to the Jews and to the satraps, deputies, and rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, to every province in its own writing and to every people in its own language. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, dates the month Sivan to the new moon of May, so that rather more than two months had now passed since the first edict went out, and glosses the lieutenants as the satraps of the realm.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley pauses over that interval of more than two months and finds in it a purpose. All that while God suffered the Jews to lie under the error of the dreadful day, he reasons, that they might be the more thoroughly humbled for their sins and purged from them; convinced too of their folly in having so often declined the offers of returning to their own land, by which neglect they lay scattered through the vast empire, an easy prey, while their brethren in Judea were better able to preserve themselves; and all this, Wesley adds, for the greater illustration of God's power and wisdom and goodness in granting so admirable and unexpected a deliverance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on one detail of the dispatch — that it was drawn up and published in the respective languages of all the provinces. Shall the subjects of an earthly prince, he asks, have his decrees in a tongue they understand, and shall God's own oracles and laws be locked up from his servants in an unknown tongue? The witnesses do not divide. They show a counter-decree issued in the fullest legal form, carried to every corner of an empire that stretched from India to Ethiopia and framed for every reader in his mother-speech; and behind the bureaucratic exactness of scribes and satraps and dated parchments they let the reader glimpse a slower providence, which had allowed the terror of Haman's day to stand two months and more precisely that a humbled people might learn, in their deliverance, whose hand had wrought it.
10:
The letters go out under the royal seal and on the swiftest beasts the empire can muster, and the witnesses, wrestling with the odd names of those animals, agree on the one thing that matters — the haste. The reformed John Gill notes that Mordecai wrote in the king Ahasuerus' name and sealed it with the king's ring, which gave the letters their authority and made them irreversible, and for this he had the king's own order. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the dispatch of the letters by posts riding on horseback and on mules, camels, and young dromedaries, the same royal relay that had once borne Haman's decree of death now bearing the decree of life.

Over the beasts themselves the witnesses confess a learned uncertainty. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns it is difficult to say what these creatures were: the word rendered mules properly means a swift chariot-horse; another is a Persian term, perhaps incurably corrupted, which Bochart derives from words meaning large mules; a third, literally sons of mares, is taken for mules bred of the mare — but there is so little agreement among the learned, and so little importance in the matter, that we may rest content to know only that they were the swiftest and hardiest beasts the country could furnish. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reaches the same end by his own philology: posts are literally the runners; the animals are rather horses of great speed, the swift beast of Micah 1:13; and of the two doubtful words he offers Gesenius's mules, the offspring of royal mares and Rawlinson's coursers of the king's stud, offspring of high-bred steeds.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the point of all this speed. These riders, he notes, were not employed in sending the former letter; but this later decree required more care and haste, that the Jews might be eased of their present fears and have time to provide for their own defence. The witnesses converge there. Whatever the exact breed of the couriers' mounts, the urgency is plain and deliberate: the same postal system, the same royal authority, the same relentless speed that had carried the sentence of extermination into every province is now turned, hoof for hoof and seal for seal, to carry the people's rescue — and the king who had once let Haman's messengers ride will now not have the answer come a day too late.
11:
The heart of the counter-decree is its grant of self-defence, and the witnesses weigh both its sweeping terms and the mercy that would temper them in the event. The reformed John Gill notes the first provision: the king granted the Jews in every city to gather themselves together in a body, sufficiently armed, in whatever quarter they should choose. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes that the decree's very words — to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish — are the same as Haman's, so that the Jews now had precisely as much authority to slay their enemies as their enemies had to slay them; and the clause naming little ones and women, harsh as it sounds, was but the ordinary custom of destroying a convicted man's whole family, included here only because the former decree against the Jews had included it, that the two edicts might be exactly matched.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses that the Jews were licensed only to stand on the defensive, not to take the initiative; it was still to risk civil war in every city of the empire, though the danger was much lessened by the numbers who now took the hint and came over to the Jews' side. And he marks a telling restraint to come: though the decree empowered them to take the spoil of their enemies for a prey, when the storm actually broke the Jews declined to take it. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reasons to the same effect — the mention of women and little ones was added to strike the greater terror into their enemies, after the laws and customs of that kingdom; yet in the execution, he notes, we read nothing of any slaughter of women or children, nor is it likely a people so indulgent to their own families would have shed such blood.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the grant in its larger frame. The decree commissioned the Jews, upon the very day appointed for their destruction, to draw together for their own defence — to stand for their life, so that whoever assaulted them did it at his peril, and even to avenge themselves on their enemies and enrich themselves with the spoil. This, Henry says, sufficiently provided for their safety, for the latter decree would be read as a tacit revocation of the former, though not in words. The witnesses do not finally divide. They grant that the edict's language is terrible, a deliberate mirror of Haman's own; but they agree that its purpose was shelter, not slaughter, and that the people armed by it would prove, in the day of battle, more sparing than the law allowed — taking their lives from the sword but not their neighbours' goods.
12:
The decree fixes its single day, and the witnesses see in that date the whole reversal of the book compressed into a number. The reformed John Gill notes what the words most need — that the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month Adar, was the very day appointed and fixed in the former letters for the destruction of the Jews. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, carrying the terms of the counter-edict across these verses, set that same day, and upon one day in all the provinces of king Ahasuerus, as the day now given to the Jews to stand and be avenged — the identical date, and the identical empire-wide reckoning, on which Haman had meant them to be swept away.

That identity is the point on which the witnesses linger, for it is no accident of the calendar. Haman had cast his lot to find the fatal day, and the day the lot fell upon is the day the king's second decree now hands back to the Jews as their own. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, tracing the design of the whole edict, marks that the Jews were commissioned to gather for their defence upon the very day which had been appointed for their ruin; the trap is not merely disarmed but turned, so that the hour of intended slaughter becomes the hour of vindication. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, reckoning the interval, observes that this decree went out more than two months after the first; and the day it named still lay some nine months off, leaving the Jews a long season to arm and prepare against the crisis that had once seemed only their doom.

The witnesses do not divide, and the bare date carries its own sermon. One day was set for the extermination of a people; that same day is now set for their preservation, and the enemies who had marked it in their calendars as a licence to kill must keep it instead as the day the Jews are armed against them. Nothing in the terror of the first decree is undone by pretending the day away; the day stands, fixed and public, exactly as Haman left it. But the meaning of the day is inverted — the appointed time of death made the appointed time of deliverance — and in that inversion, worked without the erasure of a single line of the first edict, the reader is shown how the God who governs the fall of the lot can leave the very letter of doom untouched and yet make it recoil upon the heads that devised it.
13:
The decree must now be made known, and the witnesses turn to its publication and to the disputed word that describes its aim. The reformed John Gill explains that a copy of the letters sent to the governors of the provinces was published to all people — its substance proclaimed by a herald, or posted up in public places, that everyone might know its contents and take care not to assault the Jews, since to do so would now be at their peril. The point of the proclamation, Gill sees, is as much warning as licence: the general knowledge of the new edict is itself a shield, for men will not lightly lift a hand against those whom the crown has armed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the phrase to avenge themselves on their enemies, and is careful to strip it of its harshest colour. The Hebrew word, he urges with Wordsworth, does not necessarily signify a violent emotion of a resentful spirit, but a steady resolve to defend the right; it is a word used even of the Almighty himself, when he rescues the oppressed, defends the right, and punishes the assailant and the oppressor. What the Jews are readied for, then, is not private revenge but the just repelling of a murderous attack — the same righteous requital that Scripture ascribes to God when he vindicates his own.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, following the edict through, reads its intent in the same defensive key: the Jews were empowered to avenge themselves upon their enemies, that is, to stand armed and ready against the day of assault, so that the assault might be broken upon them. The witnesses converge, and the verse yields a quiet but important distinction. The people are not turned loose to hatred; they are published to the empire as a nation henceforth to be let alone, and readied only to answer force with force on the one day their enemies had chosen. The word that our ears hear as vengeance the witnesses hear as defence and just recompense — a resolve to preserve the innocent and repel the guilty, of a piece with the justice of the God who defends the oppressed. The proclamation that had once gone out to doom them now goes out, in the same imperial voice and to the same provinces, to guard them; and its publication to all people is itself a large part of the deliverance, turning the very publicity that had exposed them into the notice that now protects them.
14:
The couriers spur away, and the witnesses ask why such headlong haste was needed when the fatal day still lay the better part of a year off. The reformed John Gill notes that the posts rode out upon the mules and camels — the swift royal beasts the Persians called by a name of their own — carrying the decree in every direction from the capital. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes that the decree was given, as the first had been, at Shushan the palace, and that in every outward respect — its form, its dispatch, its royal seal — this edict was the exact mirror of the former; only its intended effect was the contrary, life where the other had carried death.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises the question the verse presses: why this haste, seeing there yet remained nearly nine months before the first edict would come into play? His answer looks to the temper of the empire. There may well have been fears, he suggests, lest the first edict, which betrayed a distinct animus of the court against the Jews, be interpreted freely according to its spirit, and its date anticipated by eager partisans who would need no official day to fall upon a hated people. The counter-decree must therefore outrun any such zeal, reaching the provinces before private malice could act upon the earlier licence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same urgency in the doubled command by which the messengers were hastened and pressed on. It was by the king's own commandment, as well as Mordecai's, that they were hurried out on their swift beasts; the king himself, Henry supposes, was in pain lest the good news come too late, and some mischief be done to the Jews by virtue of the former decree before the notice of this one could arrive. It was no time to trifle, he says, when so many lives hung in the balance. The witnesses do not divide. They read the breakneck speed of the dispatch not as mere ceremony but as the measure of the danger: a written word of death was already loose in the world and could not be recalled, so a written word of deliverance had to chase it down through every province and reach each threatened community before the fear it answered could harden into slaughter. The haste of the horsemen is the visible sign of how narrow, even now, the margin of rescue was felt to be.
15:
The scene lifts from parchment to pageantry, and the witnesses watch Mordecai come out from the king transformed. The reformed John Gill notes simply that he went out from the royal presence and walked or rode about the city to show himself to his friends. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the change in its full contrast: but lately Mordecai was in sackcloth and all the Jews in sorrow; now here is Mordecai in purple and all the Jews in joy, the very reversal sung in Ps. 30:5. Having obtained the order for his people's relief, he laid aside his mourning weeds and put on the royal apparel — robes of blue and white, fine linen and purple, and a great crown of gold. These things, Henry says, are worth notice only as they were marks of the king's favour and the fruit of God's favour to his church; and it is well with a land when the ensigns of dignity are made the ornaments of serious piety.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the finery: the blue and white he takes for stripes interchanged, or a garment faced and bordered with white fur, and the great crown for a large turban ornamented with gold and jewels; the fine linen, the byssus of the ancients, he traces to the beard of a great Mediterranean muscle. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the word for this crown is not the one used of the royal diadem, and that the tunic was of purple striped with white; while John Wesley observes that such a crown the chief Persian princes were permitted to wear, though with a plain distinction from the king's own.

But over the city's joy the witnesses genuinely divide. Henry reads Shushan's gladness as the honest relief of a place that promises itself better times now that so good a man is trusted with power — for when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice, and when the wicked perish there is shouting. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley too reads it kindly: not the Jews only but the greater part of the citizens rejoiced, men who by the very law of nature abhorred Haman's bloody counsels and took a complacency in acts of mercy. Ellicott, however, judges the crowd more cynically: the tide of royal favour had turned, and the mob of Susa, like the populace of any age, shouted with the winning side and would as gladly have hooted had they seen Mordecai led to execution — even as the throng that cried Hosanna to our Lord soon cried Crucify. Clarke stands nearer Ellicott, remarking dryly that Haman had been too proud to be popular, and few lamented his fall. So the same rejoicing streets are read now as the joy of honest men at the triumph of virtue, now as the fickle cheer of a crowd that loves only success.
16:
From the capital the joy spreads to the whole people, and the witnesses dwell on the fourfold word that measures it. The reformed John Gill reads the opening the Jews had light as prosperity set over against the darkness of the adversity in which they had lain — or, as the words that follow explain it, a lightsomeness and cheerfulness of spirit. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the figure: light here, a rare form, is an image for prosperity, and the closing honour is the esteem shown the Jews in the general joy at the prevention of their threatened destruction — light and gladness, delight and honour, heaped up together to weigh the greatness of the change.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the piled synonyms the same way, as expressing one thing by many words to denote the sheer greatness of the joy; and he catches the sharp reversal in the last of them — honour now, instead of the contempt under which the Jews had so long lain. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into the pattern of the psalms: the Jews, but a little before under a dark cloud, dejected and disgraced, now had light and gladness, joy and honour, a feast and a good day. Thus are God's people sometimes made to sow in tears that they may reap in so much the more joy, and the suddenness and strangeness of the turn only added to their gladness, so that they were like those that dream, their mouths filled with laughter, as in Ps. 126:1.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse stands as the still centre of the book's great reversal. Every word in it answers a former sorrow: light for their darkness, gladness for their mourning, joy for their dread, honour for their contempt. The people who had been marked out for slaughter, who had fasted and wept and put on sackcloth, are now clothed inwardly in the very opposites of their grief. The witnesses let the reader feel that this is no mere change of fortune but a deliberate overturning, wrought by a hand that had let the darkness gather only to make the light more welcome; and they hear, beneath the plain historical notice, the older confession that weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. What Haman had prepared as a day of terror the Jews now keep as a day of light, and the fourfold gladness of the verse is the measure of how completely their night has broken into day.
17:
The gladness runs out to the farthest provinces, and with it comes a stranger fruit — a wave of conversions the witnesses read very differently. The reformed John Gill notes that wherever the king's commandment and decree came, to every province and city where any Jews were, there was joy and gladness. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the feast-day gladness set against the grief and lamentation Haman's edict had caused, and turn to the closing wonder: many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell upon them. This conversion, Keil cautions, is not to be explained, as some would have it, merely as a change of religion undertaken for security's sake, to court the queen's favour in dread of Mordecai's power; that may have been the motive with some in Susa, but the greater number, he judges, were moved by more than fear.

Here the witnesses openly divide over the worth of these new proselytes. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is frankly skeptical: converts made for fear were a species not likely to bring much honour to true religion, and the sacred historian states only the plain fact that they professed Judaism for fear of the Jews, whether they held to it afterward or not. Clarke turns the case into a maxim — only the Gospel admits no coercion for the spread of its doctrine, being a spiritual system propagated by spiritual means alone, so that were Christ's kingdom of this world his servants would fight, as he told Pilate in John 18:36. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same conversions far more hopefully: many of the people of the land, the sober and well-inclined, were proselyted to the Jewish faith, renounced their idols, and worshipped the true God; Haman had thought to extirpate the Jews, and behold their numbers are increased and many added to the church. When the Jews had joy and gladness, Henry observes, then many became Jews, for the holy cheerfulness of God's people is a great ornament to their profession and invites others in.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the fact soberly — they embraced the religion of the Jews as proselytes — and leaves the motives where the text leaves them. So the witnesses close the chapter around a real question they do not wholly resolve: whether this great ingathering was the timid submission of men who feared the winning side, or a true turning drawn by the manifest favour of God upon his people. Clarke suspects the former, Henry hopes the latter, Keil allows both while leaning past mere fear; and the honest tension is left standing, that a deliverance which multiplied the people of God did so through hearts of every quality, some seeking only safety and some, it may be, finding at last the living God whose hand had just been so plainly shown.
